name: Exposure Value at ISO
description: Calculates the exposure value at a given ISO from the aperture (f-number N) and shutter time t. The first term log2(N^2/t) is EV at ISO 100, and log2(iso/100) shifts it for the actual sensitivity.
notes: Shutter time t is in seconds. EV increases by 1 for each halving of light (one stop). Higher ISO lowers the required EV, so the term is subtracted.

name: Near Limit of Depth of Field
description: Gives the nearest distance in sharp focus (the near limit of the depth of field) from the hyperfocal distance H, the focused subject distance s, and the focal length f. Everything from this distance back to the far limit appears acceptably sharp.
notes: All lengths must use the same unit; here f is in metres like H and s. H itself depends on aperture and circle of confusion, computed separately.

name: Far Limit of Depth of Field
description: Gives the farthest distance in sharp focus (the far limit of the depth of field) from the hyperfocal distance H, the focused subject distance s, and the focal length f. The scene stays acceptably sharp from the near limit out to this distance.
notes: When the subject distance equals or exceeds the hyperfocal distance, the denominator reaches zero or turns negative, meaning the far limit is at infinity. Keep all lengths in the same unit.

name: Depth of Field (Approximate)
description: Estimates the total depth of field using the approximation 2·s²·N·c/f², valid when the subject distance s is well short of the hyperfocal distance. Depth grows with subject distance squared and aperture number, and shrinks with focal length squared.
notes: This is a small-distance approximation and overestimates near the hyperfocal distance. Circle of confusion c and focal length f use the same length unit as s (metres here).

name: Aperture Diameter (Entrance Pupil)
description: Calculates the effective aperture diameter (entrance pupil) as focal length f divided by the f-number N. This is the physical light-gathering opening the f-number represents for a given focal length.
notes: The f-number is defined as f divided by this diameter, so smaller N gives a larger opening. Result shares the focal length unit (mm here).

name: Angle of View
description: Gives the angle of view in degrees for a sensor dimension d and focal length f, using 2·atan(d/(2f)) converted from radians. It describes how wide a scene the lens captures along that sensor edge or diagonal.
notes: Sensor dimension and focal length must share a unit (mm). Choose d as width, height, or diagonal to get the corresponding horizontal, vertical, or diagonal angle. This is a thin-lens approximation ignoring focus distance.

name: 35mm-Equivalent Focal Length
description: Converts an actual lens focal length to its 35mm-equivalent by multiplying by the sensor crop factor. This gives the focal length a full-frame camera would need for the same angle of view.
notes: The crop factor is the ratio of the full-frame diagonal to the sensor diagonal (about 1.5 for APS-C, 2 for Micro Four Thirds). Result keeps the input length unit (mm).

name: Crop Factor from Sensor Diagonal
description: Computes the crop factor by dividing the full-frame (35mm) sensor diagonal of 43.27 mm by the given sensor diagonal. The result shows how much a smaller sensor multiplies effective focal length relative to full frame.
notes: Sensor diagonal must be entered in millimetres for the 43.27 constant to apply. A diagonal equal to 43.27 mm gives a crop factor of 1 (full frame).

name: Guide Number (Flash)
description: Calculates a flash guide number as the product of the f-number N and the flash-to-subject distance dist. The guide number summarises a flash unit's power for correct exposure at a reference ISO.
notes: The guide number carries the distance unit (metres here) and is tied to a specific ISO, usually 100. Compare only guide numbers stated for the same ISO and distance unit.

name: Flash Range from Guide Number
description: Finds the maximum flash-to-subject distance for correct exposure by dividing the guide number GN by the chosen f-number N. Opening the aperture (smaller N) extends the usable flash range.
notes: The result is in the distance unit the guide number was defined with (metres here) and assumes the guide number's reference ISO. Real range also depends on subject reflectance.

name: Guide Number ISO Scaling
description: Rescales a flash guide number from a reference ISO to a target ISO by multiplying by the square root of the ISO ratio. Doubling ISO increases the guide number by a factor of about 1.41.
notes: Only the ISO ratio matters, so both ISO values may use any consistent scale. The scaled guide number keeps the distance unit of the original.

name: Handheld Shutter Speed Limit
description: Estimates the slowest handheld shutter time before camera shake blurs the image, as the reciprocal of the 35mm-equivalent focal length (focal length f times crop factor). Longer lenses demand faster shutter speeds.
notes: This is the classic 1/focal-length rule using effective focal length; the numeric result is a shutter time in seconds. Image stabilisation allows slower speeds than this guideline suggests.

name: Sunny 16 Shutter Speed
description: Gives the shutter time for the Sunny 16 rule as the reciprocal of the ISO speed, the correct exposure in bright sunlight at aperture f/16. For ISO 100 this yields about 1/100 s.
notes: Valid only at aperture f/16 in direct front sunlight; other apertures or lighting need adjustment. The result is a shutter time in seconds.

name: Field of View Width (Subject)
description: Calculates the real-world width covered at the subject plane from the subject distance, sensor width, and focal length, using dist·sensor/f. It tells how wide a scene fits in frame at that distance.
notes: Subject distance is in metres while sensor width and focal length are in millimetres; the ratio sensor/f is dimensionless, so the result comes out in the distance unit (metres). Thin-lens approximation.

name: Optical Magnification (Object Distance)
description: Computes the optical magnification of a thin lens from focal length f and object distance s, as f/(s−f). The value is the ratio of image size to object size.
notes: Object distance must exceed the focal length for a real, focused image; s equal to f gives infinite magnification. Focal length and object distance use the same unit, and the result is dimensionless.

name: Effective f-number (Macro)
description: Gives the effective f-number in close-up work as the marked f-number N multiplied by (1 + magnification m). Lens extension for macro focusing raises the effective f-number and reduces the light reaching the sensor.
notes: At 1:1 magnification (m = 1) the effective f-number doubles, a two-stop light loss. This applies to unit-focusing lenses; internal-focus designs differ.

name: Bellows Extension Factor
description: Computes the exposure correction factor for lens extension in close-up work as (1 + magnification m)². Exposure must be multiplied by this factor, or extended by its log base 2 in stops, to compensate for light loss.
notes: At 1:1 magnification the factor is 4, meaning two stops of extra exposure. This assumes a lens that focuses by extension; the result is a dimensionless multiplier.

name: Circle of Confusion (Zeiss Formula)
description: Estimates the acceptable circle of confusion for a sensor using the Zeiss formula, sensor diagonal divided by 1730. This sets the blur-spot threshold used in depth-of-field and hyperfocal calculations.
notes: Sensor diagonal is in millimetres, so the circle of confusion comes out in millimetres. The divisor 1730 reflects a standard viewing and enlargement assumption; other conventions use different values.

name: Airy Disk Diameter (Diffraction)
description: Calculates the diameter of the Airy disk from wavelength lambda and f-number N, as 2.44·lambda·N. This diffraction-limited spot size sets the smallest resolvable detail at a given aperture.
notes: Wavelength and result share the same unit (mm here). When the Airy disk exceeds the circle of confusion or pixel pitch, stopping down further softens the image (diffraction limiting).

name: Diffraction Cutoff Frequency
description: Gives the diffraction cutoff spatial frequency as the reciprocal of wavelength times f-number, 1/(lambda·N). Above this frequency a diffraction-limited lens transmits no contrast.
notes: With wavelength in millimetres the result is in line pairs per millimetre. Stopping down (larger N) lowers the cutoff, reducing the finest resolvable detail.

name: Equivalent Shutter Speed (Aperture Change)
description: Finds the shutter time that keeps exposure constant after changing the aperture, scaling the original time t1 by (N2/N1)². Since light falls with the square of the f-number, closing down requires a proportionally longer exposure.
notes: This holds exposure fixed at unchanged ISO; it does not account for reciprocity failure at very long times. Result is a shutter time in the same unit as t1 (seconds).

name: Equivalent ISO (Exposure Match)
description: Computes the ISO needed to match a reference exposure after changing both aperture and shutter time, scaling ISO1 by (N2/N1)² and by t1/t2. It keeps overall brightness constant across the new settings.
notes: Both aperture ratio and shutter ratio are dimensionless, so any consistent units work. Closing the aperture or shortening the shutter raises the required ISO.

name: EV from Scene Luminance
description: Derives the exposure value from scene luminance L and ISO speed using log2(L·iso/12.5), where 12.5 is the standard reflected-light meter calibration constant. Brighter scenes and higher ISO both raise the EV.
notes: Luminance must be in candela per square metre for the 12.5 constant to apply. This EV is referenced to ISO 100 scaling via the ISO term; the 12.5 value follows common metering standards.

name: Stops Between Two f-numbers
description: Computes the exposure difference in stops between two apertures as 2·log2(N2/N1). Because light scales with the inverse square of the f-number, each doubling of N2/N1 corresponds to two stops.
notes: A positive result means N2 is the smaller aperture (less light); a negative result means more light. The f-numbers are dimensionless, so only their ratio matters.

name: Pixel Pitch
description: Calculates the pixel pitch as the sensor width (in mm, converted to micrometres via ×1000) divided by the horizontal pixel count. It is the centre-to-centre spacing of adjacent photosites.
notes: Sensor width is entered in millimetres and the result is in micrometres. This assumes square pixels evenly spanning the sensor width, without gaps or non-imaging borders.
